 Disclosure: As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases. I also earn a commission from some other retailers, including BLUETTI and EcoFlow (through CJ). You pay the same. 
 The weather app turns orange. Your neighbor is already dragging a gas can to the garage. You just want the phones charged, the router up, and maybe a lamp so nobody trips over the dog.
 Good news: you don’t need a $2,000 box for that. Five portable power stations were listed at $500 or less on their makers’ own U.S. stores when we checked on September 29, 2026. A portable power station is a big rechargeable battery with real wall outlets on it. Search engines like to call it a “solar generator.” Same thing. The “solar” part is a panel you buy separately.
 This is a buyer’s guide, not a lab test. We haven’t run these units ourselves. Every number below comes from the maker’s own spec page (or the live Amazon title where the maker’s page left a blank, and we say so when that happens). Prices are the maker’s list price on that date. Prices move, especially around storm season and sales.
 Two quick words first: Wh (watt-hours) is how big the gas tank is. W (watts) is how hard you can push the pedal at one time. You need enough of both.

 How we sourced this 
 Prices on these move a lot in November. Our Black Friday power station deals guide explains when sales started last year and how to spot a fake “was” price.
 Quick picks
 Best overall under $500: Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 . 1,024 Wh and the most steady output in the group (2,000 W). $499.99 on Anker’s store.
 Best for fast wall recharging before the storm: EcoFlow DELTA 3 Classic . 1,024 Wh, 1,800 W, 0–80% in about 45 minutes on wall power (EcoFlow’s claim). $499 on EcoFlow’s store.
 Lightest 1 kWh pick with the most solar headroom: BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 . 1,024 Wh, 25 lb, up to 1,000 W of solar input. $489 on BLUETTI’s store.
 Best small station you can grow later: EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus . 286 Wh, 10.4 lb, add-on batteries up to 858 Wh. $299 on EcoFlow’s store.
 Cheapest “keep the phones and router alive” box: Jackery Explorer 300 v2 . 288 Wh, 8.16 lb. $279 on Jackery’s store.
 Want bigger boxes, no price cap? See our main hub: Best Solar Generators and Portable Power Stations (2026) .

 LiFePO4 = lithium iron phosphate, a battery type that trades a little weight for a lot more charge cycles. LFP is the same thing, shorter. 
 Best overall under $500: Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2
 If you only buy one box, this is the one to look at first. It sits right at the $500 line on Anker’s store ($499.99 on September 29, 2026) and packs the most muscle of the group.
 1,024 Wh of storage.
 2,000 W steady AC output, 3,000 W peak.
 Up to 600 W of solar input (11–60 V) through an XT60i port.
 4,000 cycles to at least 80% capacity, per Anker.
 About 10 ms UPS switchover. UPS means if the wall power drops, it takes over fast enough that many devices never notice.
 24.9 lb . Five-year warranty listed in Anker’s spec data.
 Who it’s for: You want one ~1 kWh box that can run a typical drip coffee maker in the morning (check its watts) and still keep the router, phones, and lamps going through a long evening.
 Honest downside: It doesn’t grow. Anker’s own FAQ says C1000 Gen 2 has no expansion battery option. If you think you’ll want more storage later, this isn’t your upgrade path. Also, Anker’s spec table leaves the battery chemistry field blank; the “LiFePO4” comes from the Amazon listing title.
 Check price on Amazon · Anker product page 
 Best for fast recharging before the storm: EcoFlow DELTA 3 Classic
 The whole trick with outage prep is to charge the station before the storm , while the wall still works. DELTA 3 Classic is built for that. EcoFlow says it goes 0–80% in about 45 minutes and full in about an hour on wall power. EcoFlow listed it at $499 on September 29, 2026.
 1,024 Wh , LFP (LiFePO4) cells.
 1,800 W rated AC, 3,600 W surge.
 X-Boost up to 2,600 W . That’s a mode for heating gadgets, not extra rated power. See the FAQ.
 Up to 500 W solar input.
 10 ms UPS switchover. EcoFlow says the app’s Storm Guard Mode “automatically activates backup power before extreme weather hits.”
 12.1 ± 0.3 kg (about 26.7 lb).
 Who it’s for: You want to wake up to a storm warning and have a full 1 kWh battery by lunch.
 Honest downside: The “5-year warranty” is really 3 years standard plus 2 more when you register in the EcoFlow app. Register the day it arrives. And we couldn’t confirm an add-on battery option for this model on EcoFlow’s page, so plan on 1,024 Wh being what you get.
 Check price on Amazon · Check price at EcoFlow 
 Lightest 1 kWh pick: BLUETTI Elite 100 V2
 Same storage as the two above, a bit lighter at 25 lb . BLUETTI listed it at $489 (down from $499) on September 29, 2026.
 1,024 Wh , LiFePO4, 4,000+ cycles to 80% per BLUETTI.
 1,800 W rated AC, 3,600 W surge.
 Power Lifting 2,700 W — like X-Boost, a mode for heaters and kettles, not rated output.
 Up to 1,000 W solar input (12–60 V, 20 A max). That’s the biggest solar door in this list.
 ≤10 ms UPS switchover. Five-year warranty in BLUETTI’s spec table.
 Who it’s for: You’ll actually carry it — up the stairs, to the truck, to the campsite — and you might build a bigger panel setup someday.
 Honest downside: That 1,000 W solar number only matters if you own roughly 1,000 W of panels, and most folks start with one 100–200 W foldable. The Amazon listing title says four AC outlets, so a power strip may end up in the kit.
 Check price on Amazon · Check price at BLUETTI 
 Best small station you can grow: EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus
 Think lunchbox, not suitcase. 10.4 lb , and EcoFlow listed it at $299 on September 29, 2026 (on a flash-sale product page, so that price may not last).
 286 Wh now, expandable to 858 Wh with EcoFlow’s EB300 (286 Wh) or EB600 (572 Wh) add-on batteries, sold separately.
 600 W rated AC, 1,200 W surge, X-Boost 1,200 W.
 LiFePO4, 3,000 cycles to 80%.
 220 W solar input.
 <10 ms UPS. EcoFlow’s warranty table lists 5 years .
 Who it’s for: You want a router-and-phones box today and the option to add more battery later without buying a whole new station.
 Honest downside: 286 Wh is small. It’s not a fridge battery. The add-on batteries cost extra, so price the whole plan before you commit.
 Check price on Amazon · Check price at EcoFlow 
 Cheapest keep-the-lights-on box: Jackery Explorer 300 v2
 The smallest and lightest here at 8.16 lb . Jackery listed it at $279 (down from $299) on September 29, 2026.
 288 Wh , LiFePO4.
 300 W rated AC, 600 W surge peak.
 100 W USB-C output — enough for most laptops.
 Jackery says UPS response is ≤0.01 s (that’s 10 ms).
 Warranty: 3+2 years . Jackery’s page words it as “3+2 Years Warranty at Jackery.com,” so check the terms if you buy somewhere else.
 Who it’s for: Phones, a router, a CPAP (check its watts), a fan, some lights. Small apartment, small budget.
 Honest downside: 300 W is a hard ceiling. No coffee maker, no hair dryer — Jackery says so itself. Its cycle rating is 4,000 cycles to 70%+ , not to 80% like the others, so it’s not an apples-to-apples number. Jackery’s spec table doesn’t print a solar-input max; its FAQ points to SolarSaga panels up to 100 W. We couldn’t find a verified Amazon.com listing for this exact model, so we link to Jackery only.

 How to choose (with easy runtime math)
 1. Add up your “must-run” watts
 Look at the label or charger brick on each thing you want running at the same time. Add them up. That total has to stay under the station’s rated watts. Not the surge. Not the boost.
 2. Guess how long, then do this math
 Hours ≈ Wh ÷ device watts × 0.85 
 The 0.85 covers the energy the station loses turning battery power into wall power. It’s a rough rule, not a promise. Real runtime depends on the device, temperature, and battery age.
 Example load (steady) 
 ~288 Wh station 
 ~1,024 Wh station 
 15 W (say, a modem + router) 
 about 16 hours 
 about 58 hours 
 60 W (say, a CPAP without heated humidifier — check yours) 
 about 4 hours 
 about 14.5 hours 
 100 W (a few lights + a fan + phone charging) 
 about 2.4 hours 
 about 8.7 hours 
 These are our own arithmetic examples using the formula above, not test results. The watts are examples; use your device’s real number. 
 Rather skip the math? Try our portable power station size calculator : add your devices, and it shows the battery size you need.
 3. Fridge? Size up.
 A fridge compressor cycles on and off, and it kicks hard when it starts. The ~300 Wh boxes aren’t fridge batteries. The ~1 kWh boxes can help for a while. For the full walkthrough, read How Long Will a Solar Generator Run a Fridge? and How Much Solar Generator Do I Need? 
 4. Plan the recharge
 Wall first, before the storm. Solar is day two, if the sky cooperates. Panels are sold separately, and each brand likes its own plug. Match the plug with Wrong Plug, Right Watts , and match the panel’s watts and volts with Best Portable Solar Panels for Power Stations .
 5. Know the limits
 None of these will run central air, a well pump, or the whole house. For bigger backup, see Best Solar Generator for Home Backup . Not sure which brand fits you? Try Jackery vs EcoFlow vs Bluetti vs Anker .
 FAQ
 Can a $500 portable power station run my refrigerator?
 The ~1 kWh models (Anker C1000 Gen 2, EcoFlow DELTA 3 Classic, BLUETTI Elite 100 V2) have enough output for many household fridges, but how many hours you get depends on how much your fridge actually uses. The ~300 Wh models aren’t built for it. Our fridge runtime guide walks through the math.
 Is “surge” the same as X-Boost or Power Lifting?
 No. Surge is a split-second burst so a motor can start. X-Boost (EcoFlow) and Power Lifting (BLUETTI) let some heating devices — kettles, hair dryers — run above the rated limit by giving them less voltage, so they run slower or cooler. Neither is the station’s rated output. Plan around rated watts.
 Can I recharge it with solar during an outage?
 Yes, if you have a panel, the right cable, and some sun. Panels aren’t included with the base models above. A “solar suitcase” is just a folding panel, not a battery. Check the station’s solar-input limit before you buy a panel; extra panel watts past that limit just go unused.
 Can I use it indoors?
 Yes. It’s a battery, so there’s no engine and no exhaust — that’s the big difference from a gas generator, which must stay outside. Follow your station’s manual for ventilation, temperature, and keeping it dry.

A 60 W mini-fridge running all night is a completely different job than a router staying alive through a ten-minute outage, which is nothing like what a traveler squeezing a power station into a carry-on needs. No single unit is best at all three.
 What this tier does well: phones, laptops, cameras, small coolers, CPAPs, and networking gear. What it doesn’t do, regardless of what the label says: microwaves, kettles, hair dryers, or anything with a compressor motor.  Portable power stations under $300 live and die on the gap between what’s printed on the box and what you actually get at your load. Nameplate capacity and rated wattage are the manufacturer’s best-case numbers; usable energy at real device loads — a laptop, a router, a cooler — runs meaningfully lower, and the difference is what we weighed.  The questions here are the ones that don’t belong to any single pick — the cross-cutting concerns that come up regardless of which unit a reader lands on.  Can any of these run a mini-fridge? Sort of — with a big asterisk on ‘run.’ A 60–80 W compressor cooler (not a thermoelectric cooler) will plug into any unit here, but how long it runs depends entirely on capacity. The Anker 535 PowerHouse, at 512 Wh, is the only unit that runs one comfortably for 7-plus hours — that’s the overnight camp use case it was built for. The 288 Wh units (Jackery 300 v2, Anker SOLIX C300) get 3–4 hours, which is a day-trip load, not an overnight one. The smaller units — the RIVER 3 at 245 Wh, the AC2P at 230 Wh, the Elite 10 at 128 Wh — are better thought of as device chargers with cooler-assist capability, not fridge power stations.
 One class-wide limit applies here: the ‘X-Boost’ or ‘Power Lifting’ figures advertised on several of these units work only on resistive heating loads and fail on motor-driven appliances like compressor fridges. Stick to rated output — 300 W for most units, 500 W for the 535 — when sizing a compressor load.
 Which of these actually works as a UPS — will my router stay online through an outage? Three units on this page have switchover speeds fast enough to keep networking gear alive through a grid blip without a reboot: the EcoFlow RIVER 3 (20 ms, independently confirmed across routers and modems), the Anker SOLIX C300 (10 ms, scope-confirmed), and the Jackery Explorer 300 v2 (20 ms, manufacturer-rated). The RIVER 3 is the pick specifically for always-on networking because it has no standby failure pattern after extended use and its GaN inverter idles at about 5 watts — low enough to make the most of its 245 Wh capacity on a light networking load. The C300 is faster and quieter but its USB-C ports auto-shut off after roughly two hours at low current, which silently kills a router or Pi running off USB-C. Getting the unit working again requires troubleshooting before it’s usable. For a trust-it-for-years station that will spend time on a shelf between trips — which is exactly how a camping and occasional-outage all-rounder gets used — that’s the one failure mode you can’t accept.
 The Jackery 300 v2 carries no equivalent storage-failure pattern, is rated to 4,000-plus cycles versus the AC2P’s roughly 3,000, and comes with a 5-year warranty. The $140 price difference buys real long-term reliability, not a spec upgrade.
 If you buy the AC2P, buy from a retailer with a clear return path and keep it cycling rather than in storage. As a frequently-used travel charger — its other role on this page — the lockout risk is much less likely to surface.
 Why is the Jackery Explorer 300 (original) not on this page? The original 300 uses lithium-ion chemistry and is rated to around 800 charge cycles — compared to 3,000–4,000 cycles for every LiFePO4 unit on this page . Owner reports document a pattern of early capacity loss and storage failure, and it carries a slow 4.5-hour recharge. The v2 replaces it in every meaningful way, and the original’s own review steers buyers to the v2 instead. There is no use case on this page where the original 300 is the better choice.
 Can I fly with any of these? Only one: the Bluetti Elite 10, at 128 Wh. It sits inside the FAA’s 100–160 Wh carry-on band, and most major airlines allow up to two units in that range with prior approval — check your carrier’s policy before flying, since approval requirements vary. Every other unit on this page exceeds 160 Wh and cannot travel in carry-on luggage under standard airline rules. The Elite 10 is also the lightest unit here at 3.97 lb, which is part of why it’s the pick for the travel segment regardless of flight status.

 If the unit lives plugged in and its job is keeping a router alive through an outage, the EcoFlow RIVER 3 is the pick — 5-watt idle draw, 20 ms switchover confirmed across networking gear, and no standby failure pattern after extended continuous use.  Price Tiers: What Changes as You Spend More
 Sub-$500 power stations roughly break into three tiers, and understanding them prevents both overspending and buying something that cannot do the job.
 Under $250 (Anker SOLIX C300, Jackery Explorer 300 Plus): 288Wh-class units built for single-device backup — phones, laptops, a CPAP for one night, or a camp light setup. Continuous output tops out around 300W, so anything with a motor or heating element is off the table.
 $250-$350 (EGO POWER+ PST1400 and similar): this tier is where "sticker price" and "real price" start to diverge.  $350-$500 (Anker SOLIX C800 Plus): the most capable tier available before crossing into 1,000Wh-class territory above $500. Expect 700-800Wh of capacity, 1,000-1,200W continuous output, and recharge times under an hour — enough for genuine light home backup, not just device charging.
 LiFePO4 vs Older Lithium-Ion Chemistry
 Every station on this list uses LiFePO4 (lithium iron phosphate) cells, and that is not a coincidence — it is now the standard chemistry at every price point because it lasts 3,000+ charge cycles compared with 500-800 for older lithium-ion cells, and it is significantly more resistant to thermal runaway. If a sub-$500 power station you are considering does not specify LiFePO4 or LFP in its listing, treat that as a red flag and check the fine print before buying. The cycle-life difference matters most if you plan to use the station regularly rather than as a once-a-year emergency backup: a LiFePO4 unit cycled daily for years will still hold a meaningful charge long after an older lithium-ion pack has degraded past usefulness.
 How Much Capacity Do You Actually Need?
 Work backward from your worst-case use, not your average use. A single overnight CPAP run needs roughly 60-100Wh; a mini-fridge cycling on and off needs 400-600Wh over 24 hours; a work laptop plus phone charging for a full day needs under 150Wh. If your primary goal is short power outages or weekend trips, 288Wh (the Anker SOLIX C300 or Jackery Explorer 300 Plus) is often enough. If you want a buffer for a fridge, CPAP, and lighting together, the 768Wh Anker SOLIX C800 Plus is the better fit. For a broader look at sizing logic across all budgets, see how to choose a portable power station , and if your needs turn out to be larger than 800Wh, our best 1000W portable power stations roundup covers the next tier up.
 Solar Charging on a Budget

The Anker SOLIX C800 Plus accepts up to 300W, cutting that recharge window roughly in half.  Common Mistakes When Buying a Budget Power Station
 The most common mistake is comparing sticker prices without checking what is included — the EGO PST1400 is the clearest example, since its $349 price excludes the batteries that make it function. The second most common mistake is ignoring AC recharge time: a station that takes 1.5-2 hours to refill is far less useful during a multi-outage week than one that recharges in under an hour. A third mistake is confusing continuous and surge wattage: a 300W station with a 600W surge rating will still trip and shut off if you plug in a device with a 700W startup draw, even briefly, so always size against continuous wattage for anything you plan to run for more than a few seconds. Finally, buyers sometimes skip checking warranty length — all four stations here carry multi-year warranties, but coverage terms and what counts as normal wear vary by brand, so it is worth reading the fine print before you need to file a claim.

The 768Wh Anker SOLIX C800 Plus can run a modern mini-fridge or briefly cycle a full-size refrigerator, but none of the stations in this price range are sized for running a full-size fridge through a multi-day outage. For that, look at 2,000Wh-class stations above $500.
 Is a cheaper power station with standard lithium-ion cells worth buying instead? Generally no. LiFePO4 cells, used in every station in this guide, last 3,000+ cycles versus 500-800 for older lithium-ion chemistry and are far safer against thermal runaway, which is why LiFePO4 has become the standard even at budget price points.
 Is the EGO POWER+ PST1400 actually a budget option? Only if you already own EGO 56V batteries. Its $349 price excludes batteries entirely, and buying enough of them from scratch to match a comparable Anker or Jackery station can push the real cost above $1,000.
 How long does a sub-$500 power station take to recharge? It varies widely: the Anker SOLIX C800 Plus and Anker SOLIX C300 both recharge via AC in under an hour, while the Jackery Explorer 300 Plus takes about 1.5 hours. Faster AC recharge matters most if you expect repeated short outages rather than one long one.

 How to Choose a Portable Power Station Under 500 Dollars
 Pick the capacity first, the output second, and everything else after that. Every other feature on the spec sheet is secondary to whether the thing can start the appliance you care about and then run it all night.
 Capacity: Watt-Hours and the Anchor Trap
 A watt-hour is stored energy. A watt is instantaneous power. A 100W device drawing from a 300Wh pack runs for about three hours in theory, and closer to two and a half once inverter losses are counted. Work out your load by multiplying each device’s watts by the hours you need it, then subtract 15 to 20 percent for conversion loss before you choose a capacity.
 Size by use case rather than by price: a phone and a laptop for a day wants 256 to 300Wh. A CPAP machine for two nights wants 400 to 512Wh. A mini fridge over a weekend wants 512Wh upward. Power tools and appliances want 768Wh or more, which is where this budget stops.
 Continuous vs Surge Output
 Continuous output is what the unit sustains. Surge is a short burst for startup. Compressor appliances such as fridges, ice makers, and air conditioners can draw three times their running wattage at startup, so a load that fits under the continuous rating can still fail to start.
 Some brands add load-management modes that claim to run higher-wattage resistive loads, such as EcoFlow X-Boost at 600W. Treat those as an assist for a hair dryer, not as a second inverter. For motors and compressors, check the surge figure against the appliance’s startup draw instead.
 LiFePO4 vs NMC Chemistry
 LiFePO4 packs here are rated from 3000 cycles up to 6000 before hitting meaningful capacity loss, which works out to roughly a decade of service. The NMC units in this list, such as the GRECELL and the MARBERO, carry fewer documented cycles and a 2-year or 12-month warranty to match.
 Cost per year is where this decision actually lands. A higher-priced LFP unit held for six years costs less per year of service than a cheaper NMC unit replaced twice in the same period. If you intend to keep the battery, pay for the chemistry.
 Ports, USB-C PD and DC Efficiency
 USB-C Power Delivery is no longer a luxury. The Explorer 300 and Explorer 1000 v2 carry 100W ports, the ALLWEI 500W carries 100W and 36W, and the Explorer 500 v2 has none at all, which is the most common complaint in its reviews.
 Prefer DC paths for DC loads. Running a CPAP, a 12V fridge, or a phone from USB-C or the car socket skips the inverter and avoids most of the 15 to 25 percent conversion loss. The same battery can deliver meaningfully more runtime, and on a 256Wh unit that difference is the whole night.
 Charging Speed and Solar Input
 Refill speed decides whether a station is practical. The EcoFlow RIVER 2 reaches full in one hour on AC, the ALLWEI 500W takes 2.5 hours, the Explorer 500 v2 hits 80 percent in 52 minutes, and the small 256 to 280Wh units typically need 3.5 to 6 hours.
 Solar input ceiling matters more than panel wattage. A nominal 200W panel delivers nothing if its open-circuit voltage sits outside the station’s window, which is why the MPPT-equipped units here outperform PWM units with the same panel. Plan on one 100W panel for a sub-300Wh unit and two for a 500Wh one, and remember the panel is a separate purchase that can cost as much as the station.
 Weight, Noise and Warranty Length
 Weight tracks capacity closely here, from 4.6 pounds for the MARBERO to 37.4 pounds for the BLUETTI AC180. Rule of thumb: under 8 pounds for a daypack, 13 to 15 for a car trunk, above 20 for a fixed indoor location.
 Noise decides whether you can sleep near it. The Explorer 500 v2 runs as low as 28 dB and the Explorer 1000 v2 has a 30 dB quiet mode, while the EcoFlow RIVER 2’s fan is audible at full charging speed. Warranty length is the best available proxy for manufacturer confidence: 5 years on the Jackery, EcoFlow, and BLUETTI units, 2 years on the ALLWEI and GRECELL units, 12 months on the MARBERO and ZeroKor.
 Airline Limits: Why Portable Is Not the Same as Carry-On
 Every unit in this roundup exceeds the passenger lithium battery allowance for carry-on travel, which caps spare batteries at 100 watt-hours with terminals protected. A 237Wh unit is not an airline-legal carry-on, and a 1152Wh one is nowhere near it. Checked baggage rules are stricter still and vary by carrier.
 For air travel, buy a compliant battery at the destination or plan to charge at the far end. For everything in this list, “portable” means car trunk, tent, or garage.
 One last safety note that applies to any battery you charge unattended: look for a battery management system with temperature and overcurrent protection, and charge on a hard surface away from anything flammable. Every unit on this list has one. That is a buying gate, not an afterthought, and it is the main reason we do not recommend unbranded marketplace units in this price band.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best budget portable power station under $500?
 The Jackery Explorer 300 is the best budget portable power station under 500 dollars for most people. It gives you 292Wh of LiFePO4 capacity, 300W of continuous output, a 100W USB-C port, and weighs 7.1 pounds, with 11273 owner ratings behind it. If you need more capacity for a CPAP machine or a fridge, the Jackery Explorer 500 v2 at 512Wh is the step up, and the BLUETTI AC180 covers whole-room outages at 1152Wh.
 Is Jackery or EcoFlow better?
 Jackery builds more capacity into the same budget, while EcoFlow refills faster and holds a longer warranty. Jackery Explorer 500 v2 gives you 512Wh with a 5-year warranty and a 10ms UPS. EcoFlow RIVER 2 gives you 256Wh with a one-hour full recharge on AC and the same 5-year warranty. Choose Jackery for runtime and choose EcoFlow for turnaround speed and app control.
 How many watts do I need in a portable power station?
 Match continuous output to the largest single appliance you plan to run, not to your battery size. A CPAP, phones, and lights need almost nothing beyond 100W. A hair dryer needs about 1200W. A small fridge or blender needs 300W to 600W continuous. Always check surge rating too, since compressor appliances can draw two to three times their running wattage at startup.
 How do I work out what size portable power station I need?
 List every device and its wattage, then multiply each by the hours you need it. Add those watt-hours together, then subtract 15 to 20 percent for inverter losses. Round up to the next standard capacity: 256Wh, 300Wh, 512Wh, or 768Wh. As a shortcut, 256 to 300Wh covers phones and laptops for a day, 400 to 512Wh covers two nights of CPAP, and 512Wh upward covers a mini fridge.
 What can a 1000W portable power station run?
 A 1000W continuous output comfortably runs a router, laptop, television, blender, space heater, and most power tools, plus a CPAP machine and a small refrigerator simultaneously. Our two 1000W-plus picks are the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 at 1070Wh and 1500W, and the BLUETTI AC180 at 1152Wh and 1800W. Micro ovens and full-size heaters still exceed that range.
 Can a portable power station under 500 dollars run a CPAP?
 Yes, and it is the most common use owners report. Run the machine from the DC or USB-C port rather than an AC inverter to skip the 15 to 25 percent conversion loss. One verified owner ran 20 hours of CPAP across three nights on a single charge of the 256Wh ALLWEI, and owners report multiple nights from the 512Wh Jackery Explorer 500 v2. Check your machine’s voltage before you buy.
 What is the difference between watts and watt-hours?
 Watts measure speed and watt-hours measure stored energy. A 100W kettle running for one hour draws 100Wh from a battery. So a 512Wh pack is theoretically good for about five hours of that kettle, minus inverter losses. Capacity decides how long the unit can run something; wattage decides whether it can start that something at all. Both numbers have to match your load.
 Final Verdict: Which Portable Power Station Should You Buy?
 The best portable power stations under 500 dollars in 2026 start with the Jackery Explorer 300. It carries 292Wh, weighs 7.1 pounds, has a 100W USB-C port, and sits on LiFePO4 cells rated past 4000 cycles, which is the best-balanced package in this category and the deepest review base to prove it.
 Buy the Jackery Explorer 500 v2 if your load is a CPAP machine, a mini fridge, or a home office, since 512Wh and a 10ms UPS handle all three. Buy the EcoFlow RIVER 2 if your window to recharge is short, because a full AC cycle in one hour beats everything else here. Buy the BLUETTI AC180 if you want whole-room outage coverage and can live with 37 pounds in one place. For pure value on CPAP runtime, the ALLWEI 300W at 256Wh is hard to argue with.
 And check the battery management system before you check anything else, especially if you plan to charge the unit unattended overnight. That single feature separates the units worth owning from the ones you should walk past.

A portable power station is a sealed battery pack with AC outlets, USB ports, and a car socket. It powers laptops, phones, lights, fans, a CPAP, a mini fridge, or a router during a blackout. Two years ago anything useful cost $500+. In 2026 the sub-$300 tier finally crossed into LiFePO4 chemistry, real 100 W USB-C charging, and capacities that actually last a night.

This guide explains the specs that decide whether a power station is worth buying, the marketing claims to ignore, and the five best units under $300 for camping, blackouts, vanlife, and home backup.

What to look for in a power station under $300
Capacity: 250–500 Wh. Watt-hours tell you how much energy is stored. 300 Wh runs a 60 W laptop for about 4 hours, a 10 W LED light overnight, or a small CPAP for 6–8 hours. Below 200 Wh is more of a large power bank than a station.
LiFePO4 (LFP) chemistry. LFP batteries last 3,000–6,000 charge cycles to 80% capacity, vs 500–800 cycles for older NMC lithium. They are also safer in heat and on the road. At this price tier, LFP is the single biggest spec upgrade.
Pure sine wave AC inverter, 300–600 W. Pure sine wave is required for sensitive electronics: laptops, CPAP machines, TVs, audio gear. Modified sine wave units are cheaper but make CPAPs and laptop chargers buzz, overheat, or refuse to run. Continuous wattage matters more than peak/surge wattage.
USB-C PD 60–100 W. A real PD port charges a modern laptop or a phone at full speed. Older units have only 18 W USB-C, which is barely useful for a laptop.
Recharge speed. Look for AC recharge in 1.5–3 hours and solar input via MPPT (60–100 W). Older units took 6–8 hours to refill, which is impractical between camping trips.
App or simple display. A clear display showing input watts, output watts, remaining percent, and estimated runtime is more useful than fancy app control. Apps are nice to have, not essential.
Weight and handle. 300 Wh stations weigh 3–5 kg with LFP. Anything claiming 500 Wh at under 4 kg is either misrated or using older NMC cells.
1. Best overall — 300 Wh LiFePO4 with 600 W AC and 100 W USB-C

The sweet spot at $280 is a 300 Wh LiFePO4 unit with a 600 W pure sine wave inverter, a 100 W USB-C PD port, two AC outlets, a car socket, and a clear LCD. It charges from empty in roughly 90 minutes on AC and accepts up to 100 W of solar input.

Use it for: weekend camping, a home office during blackouts, road trips with a laptop and phone, charging an e-bike battery in a pinch. A 60 W laptop runs about 4 hours, a phone charges 20+ times, and a 10 W LED string runs for 25+ hours.

2. Best ultra-portable — 250 Wh, 1.8 kg, fits in a backpack

If you hike, bikepack, or travel, weight matters more than capacity. A compact 250 Wh LFP unit at 1.8 kg with a soft-grip handle and a single 300 W AC outlet plus 60 W USB-C is the right pick for ~$200. You give up the second AC outlet and some recharge speed, but you can carry it.

It runs a laptop for 3 hours, a CPAP for 5–6 hours in DC mode, or a string of festival lights all night. Use it for solo camping, photo trips, and as a backpack battery for off-grid work sessions.

CPAP machines draw about 30–60 W and need silent power. The best CPAP-friendly unit at $300 has 500 Wh of LFP capacity, a 12 V DC output for direct CPAP cables (skipping the inverter for higher efficiency), and a fan that does not spin when DC load is low.

4. Best for solar setups — strong MPPT input

If you plan to recharge from a solar panel, the MPPT input rating is the spec that matters. A station that accepts 100 W of solar (open-circuit voltage up to 24 V) recharges a 300 Wh battery in 4–6 hours of good sun. Pair it with a 100 W foldable panel for vanlife, off-grid cabins, or extended camping.

Skip stations that only accept 30 W of solar — they exist, they are cheap, and they take days to refill from sun alone.

At $150 you can still get a 200 Wh NMC unit with a 200 W AC inverter, two USB-A ports, one 45 W USB-C, and a car socket. It is fine for occasional camping, a single laptop charge, or short blackouts. Do not expect it to last more than 500 full cycles, and do not leave it in a hot car for months.

If you will use the unit weekly or rely on it for medical equipment, spend the extra $100–150 for an LFP model. The longer cycle life pays for itself.

What you can actually run, and for how long
Phone (10 Wh per full charge): 25–50 charges from a 300 Wh station.
Laptop (60 W draw): 4 hours from 300 Wh, 7 hours from 500 Wh.
CPAP without humidifier (40 W avg): 6–7 hours from 300 Wh, 10–11 hours from 500 Wh.
Mini fridge (45 W cycling, ~15 W average): 18–20 hours from 300 Wh.
WiFi router (10 W): 25+ hours from 300 Wh — useful in a blackout for work-from-home.
LED camping lights (5–10 W): a full weekend.
Hair dryer or kettle (1200–1800 W): will not run, period. These are over the inverter limit at this price tier.
Common mistakes to avoid
Confusing watts and watt-hours. A 600 W inverter says how much power it can deliver at once. 300 Wh says how much total energy it stores. Both matter.
Believing peak/surge wattage numbers. "1200 W peak" means it can briefly handle a startup spike, not run a 1200 W appliance. Continuous wattage is the real limit.
Buying modified sine wave for a CPAP. Many CPAPs throw error codes or buzz on modified sine wave. Always confirm pure sine wave for medical and audio gear.
Skipping LFP to save $50. Older NMC cells degrade faster, especially in hot cars and garages. LFP is the single best long-term upgrade.
Underestimating recharge time. A 300 Wh station that takes 8 hours to refill on AC is annoying. Prioritize units with 1.5–3 hour AC recharge.
Forgetting cable losses. Long extension cords and cheap inverters waste 10–20% of stored energy as heat. Plan capacity with that in mind.

 Best Portable Power Station Under $500 (2026) — Compared & Ranked
 You don’t need to spend a thousand dollars to get a capable portable power station. The sub-$500 bracket has gotten remarkably competitive, with LiFePO4 batteries, fast charging, and 1000+Wh capacity now available at prices that were unthinkable two years ago.
 Our top pick under $500 is the Anker Solix C1000 Gen 2 Check Price on Amazon , which regularly drops from $649 to $449 during frequent Anker sales. At sale price, it’s the most capable power station you can buy under $500 — period. But there are also strong options at the best options at every price tier from $149 to $499.

 1. Anker Solix C1000 Gen 2 — Best Overall Under $500
 Why it’s #1: This is a premium power station that happens to go on sale constantly. Anker runs promotions roughly every 4-6 weeks, and the C1000 Gen 2 regularly hits $449 — sometimes lower. At that price, nothing else comes close.
 Check Price on Amazon 
 The MSRP is $649, which is technically above our $500 threshold. But Anker’s sale cadence is so predictable that paying full price is a choice, not a necessity. Set a price alert on CamelCamelCamel or Keepa and wait for the next drop.
 What you get for under $500: 
 1056Wh of LiFePO4 capacity — more than any competitor at this price
 2000W continuous output handles blenders, griddles, mini fridges, and power tools
 49-minute full charge — the fastest in any 1000Wh unit
 4000-cycle battery rated for 10+ years
 600W solar input for serious off-grid use
 10ms UPS switchover for home backup duty
 Who should wait for this: Anyone who doesn’t need a power station this week. If you can wait 2-4 weeks for the next sale, this is hands-down the best value in the entire portable power station market.
 Verdict: The best power station under $500 — if you buy it on sale. Set a price alert and be patient.
 2. Anker Solix C800 Plus — Best Always-Available Mid-Range
 Why it’s on this list: At $499 every day (no sale required), the C800 Plus offers a strong mid-range option with 768Wh capacity and 1600W output. It’s the reliable buy when you need a power station now.
 Check Price on Amazon 
 What you get for $499: 
 768Wh LiFePO4 capacity — enough for a weekend camping trip or 8+ hours of fridge backup
 1600W output runs most common appliances
 22 lbs — lighter than the 1000Wh class
 Fast AC charging under an hour
 Clean Anker build quality and 5-year warranty
 What could be better: 
 768Wh is a noticeable step down from the C1000’s 1056Wh. For a day trip or a single overnight, it’s plenty. For extended use, you’ll feel the smaller capacity.
 1600W output won’t run high-draw appliances like space heaters at full blast.

 5. EcoFlow River 3 — Best Under $200

 The EcoFlow River 3 costs just $20 more and gives you 41Wh more capacity, double the output, and IP54 weather resistance. Hard to justify the AC2A unless you absolutely can’t spend $169.
 Who should buy this: Buyers on the tightest possible budget who want LiFePO4 battery chemistry. Emergency kit additions where minimal power is better than none.
 Verdict: The price floor for LiFePO4. Functional but limited — spend the extra $20 on the EcoFlow River 3 if you possibly can.
 How We Chose These
 For a budget roundup, value is everything. We calculated the effective cost per watt-hour for each station, then balanced that against output wattage, charging speed, build quality, and brand reliability. A station that costs less per Wh but falls apart in a year isn’t a good value. We only included LiFePO4 battery stations because the longevity advantage (3000+ cycles vs ~500 for lithium-ion ) makes them the better long-term investment even at a slightly higher upfront cost.
 We also tracked real sale prices, not just MSRPs. Several stations on this list have “regular” prices above $500 but spend more time on sale than at full price.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Is it worth buying a cheap power station vs. spending more?
 Depends on your use case. A $169 River 3 handles phone charging and camp lights perfectly — spending $800 more for a 1000Wh unit would be wasteful if that’s all you need. But if you want to run a mini fridge, power tools, or a CPAP, the compact budget stations physically can’t do the job. Buy based on what you’ll actually plug into it, not on getting the biggest number for the least money.
 How often do portable power stations go on sale?
 Major brands run sales frequently. Anker and EcoFlow drop prices roughly every 4-6 weeks, with the biggest discounts during Amazon Prime Day (July), Black Friday, and brand-specific anniversary sales. Jackery and Bluetti follow similar patterns. We recommend setting price alerts on CamelCamelCamel or Keepa for any station over $300 — you’ll almost always find it cheaper within a month.
 Should I buy a bigger station or two smaller ones?
 One bigger station is almost always better. You get more usable capacity (no losses from managing two units), simpler setup, higher output from a single unit, and easier transport. The exception: if you need power in two locations simultaneously (campsite + car, or two rooms during an outage), two smaller units make sense.
 What’s the most important spec when buying on a budget?
 Capacity (Wh) and output (W), in that order. Capacity determines how long it runs. Output determines what it can run. A 1000Wh station with only 300W output has great endurance but can’t power anything substantial. A 200Wh station with 2000W output can power almost anything — for about ten minutes. You need enough of both for your specific use case. Our guide on what size portable power station do I need walks through the math.

 What You Get (and Don't) Under $500
 At this price point, expect 250–300 Wh of LiFePO4 capacity, up to about 600W of AC output, and one to three AC outlets on most units (the DC-only Anker C300 DC has none). That's enough for phones, laptops, small camp lights, a CPAP machine overnight, or a mini fridge for several hours — but not a full home-backup load like a sump pump or window AC unit.
 The biggest trade-off versus pricier units isn't capacity — it's solar input . Budget units typically cap around 100–200W of solar charging, meaning a full recharge from panels alone takes most of a sunny day. If solar charging speed matters more than price, look at our camping guide for mid-tier units with faster solar input.
 All three picks below use LiFePO4 (LFP) battery chemistry rather than older NMC lithium — this matters because LiFePO4 cells handle roughly 2,500–3,500 charge cycles before dropping to 80% capacity, versus 500–1,000 for NMC. At a similar price, always prefer LiFePO4.
 LiFePO4 vs NMC: Why It Matters at the Budget Tier
 At the under-$500 price point, you'll find both LiFePO4 and older NMC lithium units. The temptation is to buy the cheaper NMC option and save a little upfront. Here is why that is usually a mistake:
 Cycle life is the biggest factor. A LiFePO4 unit rated for 3,000 cycles at 80% depth of discharge will last 8+ years if you use it every weekend. An NMC unit rated for 500 cycles at the same DoD will be noticeably degraded after 1–2 years of regular use. Over the life of the product, the LiFePO4 unit's cost-per-cycle is dramatically lower even if the upfront price is slightly higher.
 Thermal stability matters for portable use. LiFePO4 chemistry is inherently more stable at high temperatures — it won't enter thermal runaway the way NMC can if damaged or exposed to extreme heat. For a generator that lives in a car trunk, camping tent, or sunny garage, that's a meaningful safety advantage.
 Storage behavior differs too. LiFePO4 batteries lose capacity much more slowly during long-term storage. If you buy a budget generator for emergency backup and only use it during power outages (potentially months apart), LiFePO4 will hold its charge and capacity far better than NMC without regular maintenance charging.
 The only scenario where NMC still makes sense at the budget tier is if you need the absolute lightest possible unit and are willing to replace it more often — but even then, the weight difference at the 250–300 Wh size is typically only a few ounces. All three of our picks below use LiFePO4, and we recommend you filter for that chemistry regardless of which unit you choose.
 Best Solar Panels to Pair with Budget Generators
 Budget solar generators typically accept 100–200W of solar input. That's enough for trickle-charging during a camping trip or topping off over a day, but not enough for a full recharge from empty in a few hours. Here's how to get the most out of solar charging on a budget unit:
 Match the brand's panel for best compatibility. Anker, Jackery, and EcoFlow all make 50–100W panels designed to pair with their budget units. These panels use proprietary connectors that work without adapters, and the folding suitcase design makes setup simple.
 A 100W panel is the sweet spot. A budget unit with 100W of solar input can fully recharge from empty in about 3–4 hours of direct sun (assuming 250–300 Wh capacity). That's fast enough to run devices at night and recharge during the day.
 Third-party panels work with the right adapter. If you already own generic solar panels (common 12V panels with MC4 connectors), you can buy an inexpensive adapter cable to connect them to most brand-name generators. Just make sure the voltage range is compatible — most budget units accept 12–28V input.
 Consider a bundled panel+generator kit. Many brands offer the generator with a compatible panel at a bundled price. If you know you'll want solar charging (and most camping users do), the bundle is usually a better value than buying separately.
 Even with a modest 50–100W panel, a budget solar generator becomes a sustainable off-grid power source for phones, tablets, a laptop, and camp lights — you just won't be running anything with a large motor or heating element for long.
 Realistic Use Cases for a Solar Generator Under $500
 A budget solar generator won't power your home during a multi-day outage or run a construction site. Here's what it will do well:
 Weekend camping trips: Phone charging, headlamps, a camp fan, a speaker, and camera batteries for 2–3 nights. With a 100W panel, fully self-sufficient off-grid.
 CPAP backup at a campsite or hotel: A 288 Wh unit runs a CPAP (without humidifier) for roughly 6–8 hours per charge — a full night's sleep with margin.
 Emergency device charging during short outages: Keep phones, tablets, laptop, and router running for 1–2 days during a brief power outage. Enough to work from home, stay informed, and keep kids entertained.
 Car camping / road trip convenience: Charge devices without running your vehicle's engine or draining its starter battery. Some units double as a jump starter or have built-in LED lights for campsite illumination.
 Tailgating and outdoor events: Run a small speaker, phone charger, and a small portable fan for several hours — a big upgrade over disposable batteries and USB power banks.
 What it won't do: Run a full-size refrigerator for more than a few hours, power a sump pump or window AC unit, or keep your whole home running through a multi-day outage. For those scenarios, step up to our home backup guide for larger-capacity units.

 Frequently Asked Questions About Budget Solar Generators
 Is a solar generator under $500 worth it? 
 Yes, for the right use case — phone/laptop charging, CPAP backup, small camp devices, and short emergency outages. These units are not sized for running home appliances like fridges for extended periods or anything with a large motor. If you need home backup, see our home backup guide for larger-capacity units.
 What's the cheapest reliable solar generator? 
 Among reputable brands, the Anker SOLIX C300 DC and Jackery Explorer 300 are consistently the best value at this price. Both use LiFePO4 cells rather than shorter-lived NMC lithium. Avoid no-name brands on Amazon with inflated capacity claims — they often exaggerate watt-hour ratings and use poor-quality cells.
 LiFePO4 vs NMC — does it matter at the budget tier? 
 Yes, significantly. LiFePO4 batteries last 2,500–3,500+ charge cycles versus 500–1,000 for NMC lithium. At a similar price, LiFePO4 is the better long-term value even though it's sometimes marginally heavier. All three of our picks use LiFePO4.
 Can a solar generator under $500 run a CPAP machine? 
 Yes. CPAP machines draw 30–60W (without humidifier), so a 288 Wh budget unit can run one for roughly 5–8 hours per charge — a full night's sleep. With the humidifier running, draw increases to 50–80W, reducing runtime to 3–5 hours. Use the 12V DC adapter if available for slightly better efficiency than AC.
 How long does a budget solar generator last per charge? 
 A 288 Wh unit will charge a smartphone roughly 20–25 times, run a 15W laptop for 15–18 hours, power a 40W camp fan for 6–7 hours, or run a mini cooler for 4–6 hours. For a CPAP without humidifier, expect one full night. Actual runtime depends on what you plug in and whether you're charging devices simultaneously.
 Can I add a solar panel to a budget generator later? 
 Yes, all three picks above have a dedicated solar input port. You can buy the generator now and add a compatible panel later when your budget allows. Just make sure the panel's voltage and connector type match the generator — check the specs before buying a panel, especially if mixing brands.
 How do budget solar generators compare to power banks? 
 A solar generator is essentially a very large power bank with built-in AC (wall-style) outlets. A typical portable power bank holds 20–30 Wh (enough for 4–6 phone charges) and only has USB outputs. A budget solar generator holds 250–300 Wh and usually has standard AC outlets (DC-only models like the Anker C300 DC are the exception), meaning it can power anything you'd plug into a wall — laptops, CPAP machines, fans, small appliances — not just USB devices.
